title: Describe a time you made a mistake that affected production: what happened, how did you fix it, and what did you do to prevent it from happening again?
shortTitle: A Mistake That Affected Production: how did you fix and prevent it?
keyPoints: Own the mistake plainly without excuses or blame-shifting.
Follow the incident order: contain, fix, communicate, prevent.
Contain the blast radius first, then correct the affected data.
Communicate honestly to stakeholders at every stage.
Build a systemic guardrail (dry-run, second approval) not just a personal promise to be careful.
Show that hiding a production mistake is far worse than the mistake itself.
The preventive control is the most important part of the answer.

s1_definition.oneliner: In production, contain first, fix second, communicate throughout, and prevent recurrence last : and own every step.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Full ownership** – Admit the mistake plainly; do not blame the requirements, the deadline, or a teammate.
- **Contain first** – Stop the bad process, disable the feature, or roll back before fixing.
- **Communicate honestly** – Keep stakeholders informed at every stage; hiding is worse than the mistake.
- **Systemic prevention** – Build a guardrail (dry-run, second approval, automated rollback) that prevents the class of mistake, not just a promise to be careful.
- **Blameless mindset** – Focus on fixing the system so humans cannot make the same error again.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a developer at National Bank of India accidentally ran a data update that set the wrong interest flag on a batch of accounts including Priya's. Fixing a production mistake is like a bank catching a wrong charge: you stop the bleeding first, correct the affected accounts, communicate honestly, and then add a control so that kind of update can never run unguarded again.

sections.s6_takeaway:
At National Bank of India, I once ran a bulk update to correct an interest flag on a set of accounts, and my filter was slightly too broad, so it touched more accounts than intended, including some it should never have affected like Priya's. The change went straight to production with no preview and no second check. It was my error, plain and simple.

My first priority was to contain the damage. I stopped further processing, identified exactly which accounts had been wrongly changed using the audit records, and reverted them to their correct state. Throughout, I kept my manager and the operations team informed, because in a bank hiding a production mistake is far worse than the mistake itself.

Once the accounts were corrected, I fixed the real root cause. The problem was not simply that I made a filter mistake : humans will always make filter mistakes. The problem was that a bulk operation on customer data could run with no preview and no confirmation. So I built a guardrail: every bulk update now runs a mandatory dry run first that reports exactly which accounts would change, and the actual change only applies after a second person explicitly confirms it.

After that, a wrong filter gets caught harmlessly in the dry run instead of in production. What I learned is that owning a production mistake means containing it calmly, communicating honestly, and then turning the lesson into a systemic control so the same class of mistake simply cannot happen again.

Remember one sentence: Own production mistakes plainly, contain first, communicate honestly, and build a systemic guardrail so the same class of error is caught before production.
